IC-Case 31 - Summary of Data Analysis

Reliability and Factor Analysis for R3 and R6

Author

Willy Su

Published

November 24, 2026

1 Data Preparation

This analysis examines the reliability and construct validity of two multi-item scales in Case 31:

  • R3: Attitude toward Employee Proficiency (Q3–Q6)
  • R6: Attitude toward Operational Effectiveness (Q31–Q34)

1.1 Variable Selection

Code 
r3_items <- efcu |>
  select(q3, q4, q5, q6)

r6_items <- efcu |>
  select(q31, q32, q33, q34)

2 R3: Attitude toward Employee Proficiency

2.1 Exploratory Factor Analysis

Exploratory factor analysis is conducted on Q3–Q6 to examine whether the four items measure a single underlying construct.

2.1.1 KMO and Bartlett’s Test

Code 
psych::KMO(r3_items)
Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin factor adequacy
Call: psych::KMO(r = r3_items)
Overall MSA =  0.78
MSA for each item = 
  q3   q4   q5   q6 
0.76 0.73 0.84 0.79

psych::cortest.bartlett(
  cor(r3_items),
  n = nrow(r3_items)
)

2.1.4 Interpretation

The KMO value of 0.78 and significant Bartlett’s test (p < 0.001) indicate that the data are suitable for factor analysis.

Factor loadings range from 0.722 to 0.923, and all communalities exceed 0.50. The one-factor solution explains 63.3% of the total variance, providing evidence of convergent validity.

However, the model fit indices suggest that the one-factor structure should be interpreted with caution. Further reliability and discriminant validity analyses are needed before confirming the composite scale.

3.1.4 Interpretation

The KMO value of 0.50 indicates marginal sampling adequacy. Although Bartlett’s test is significant (p < 0.001), most factor loadings and communalities are low.

The one-factor solution explains only 31.4% of the variance and produces an ultra-Heywood case. These results indicate weak convergent validity and do not support creating a composite scale at this stage.

4 Combined Factor Analysis

4.1 Discriminant Validity

A combined factor analysis is conducted on Q3–Q6 and Q31–Q34 to examine whether employee proficiency and operational effectiveness represent two distinct constructs.

4.1.1 Parallel Analysis

Code 
combined_items <- cbind(r3_items, r6_items)
Code 
set.seed(123)

combined_parallel <- psych::fa.parallel(
  combined_items,
  fa = "fa",
  fm = "minres",
  n.iter = 100
)
Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  2  and the number of components =  NA

4.1.3 Factor Diagram

Code 
psych::fa.diagram(combined_efa)

4.1.4 Interpretation

Parallel analysis suggests a two-factor structure. R3 items load strongly on the same factor, while R6 items show weak and inconsistent loadings.

The factor correlation is 0.401. However, the ultra-Heywood case and weak R6 loadings indicate that discriminant validity is not fully supported.

5.3 Reliability Summary

Code 
reliability_summary <- data.frame(
  Scale = c("R3", "R6"),
  Items = c(4, 4),
  Cronbach_Alpha = c(
    r3_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    r6_alpha$total$raw_alpha
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  reliability_summary,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Reliability Analysis Summary"
)
Reliability Analysis Summary
Scale Items Cronbach_Alpha
R3 4 0.866
R6 4 0.472

5.4 Interpretation

R3 demonstrates good internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.866). Removing any item reduces reliability, supporting the retention of all four items.

R6 demonstrates low internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.472). Removing individual items does not substantially improve reliability. Therefore, the R6 items should be analyzed individually.

6 Composite Scale Decision and Conclusion

6.1 R3: Employee Proficiency

R3 demonstrates good internal consistency (alpha = 0.866) and strong factor loadings. Despite limitations in model fit, Q3–Q6 can be combined into a composite scale by averaging the four items, with caution.

6.2 R6: Operational Effectiveness

R6 demonstrates low reliability (alpha = 0.472) and weak convergent validity. Therefore, Q31–Q34 should be analyzed individually rather than combined into a composite scale.

6.3 Conclusion

The results support using a composite scale for R3 with caution, but not for R6. Discriminant validity is only partially supported.
